= Biomarker Discovery and Prioritisation

A translational team is asked which biomarkers belong on a panel for a given indication. The candidates already exist in the public domain - the hard part is ranking them by evidence, measurability and specificity before committing to an assay.

== Introduction

Biomarker programmes rarely fail for lack of candidates. Public evidence already contains tens of thousands of biomarker claims: somatic and germline variants from clinical-genomics curation, risk alleles from genome-wide association studies, protein abundance markers from proteomics resources, metabolites from newborn-screening reference sets, and the literature behind all of it.

What is missing is triage. Every source uses its own identifiers (NCBI Gene, UniProtKB, LOINC, dbSNP), its own disease vocabulary (Disease Ontology, MONDO, free text), and its own idea of what constitutes "the biomarker" - sometimes a gene, sometimes a specific mutation in that gene, sometimes the direction of change of a protein level in serum. Two records that describe the same analyte can share no field at all.

So the question _"what should we measure for this indication, and how confident are we?"_ turns into weeks of manual reconciliation in spreadsheets. The reconciliation is expensive, it is done by a small number of people who hold the mappings in their heads, and it is discarded as soon as the next indication comes up. The cost is not compute; it is the months between the question and a defensible shortlist.

== Scenario

A diagnostics team is scoping a blood-based test for breast cancer. Before designing an assay they need answers to five questions:

. *What is already claimed?* Which biomarkers are reported for this disease, what do they assess, and in what clinical role - diagnostic, prognostic, monitoring, predictive?
. *What can we actually measure?* Which candidates have been reported in serum, plasma, blood or urine, rather than in a tissue sample that requires a biopsy?
. *How deep is the evidence?* How many independent publications and source databases stand behind each candidate?
. *How specific is it?* An analyte that marks eighteen other diseases will not discriminate. Which candidates are promiscuous?
. *What are we missing?* The literature describes markers that no curated database has yet formally linked to this disease. Can they be surfaced?

Every one of these is a question about _relationships_ - between a marker and its evidence, between an analyte and every disease it has been associated with, between a disease and its parents in an ontology. In a relational schema each requires a different set of joins across sources that were never designed to be joined. Three concrete obstacles show up immediately:

* *The disease is named several ways.* "breast cancer", "breast carcinoma", "malignant neoplasm of breast" and `DOID:1612` all appear. Any query that filters on a disease string silently under-reports.
* *The same analyte appears under multiple identifiers.* Prostate specific antigen is present as both `LOINC:10886-0` and `LOINC:12841-3`; RASSF1 exists as `NCBI:11186` under two different entity types because two source datasets disagreed about whether it is a gene or a protein.
* *The evidence is a citation, not a value.* Judging a candidate means counting distinct supporting publications and distinct source databases, which is a graph aggregation, not a column.

== Solution

Model the biomarker itself as a node rather than a row, and connect it to everything that gives it meaning.

Once a `Biomarker` is linked to the entity it assesses, the condition it indicates, the specimen it is measured in, the clinical role it plays and the publications and database records that support it, the five questions above collapse into short traversals:

* *Evidence depth* is the count of distinct `Publication` and `Xref` nodes reachable from a candidate.
* *Specificity* is the count of _other_ `Condition` nodes reachable from the same assessed entity - a single hop out and back.
* *Vocabulary drift* stops mattering, because conditions are Disease Ontology terms connected by `IS_A`. Asking for "organ system cancer" rolls up every descendant automatically, whatever each source called it.
* *Literature reach* extends beyond curated links, because publications carry MeSH indexing and vector embeddings. Semantic similarity finds papers - and therefore candidate markers - that no source has yet connected to the disease.

This page builds that graph from https://data.biomarkerkb.org/[BiomarkerKB], an NIH https://commonfund.nih.gov/dataecosystem[Common Fund Data Ecosystem] project that integrates biomarker data from many public sources. Loaded in full, release v-3.2.2 produces a graph of *488,624 nodes and 1,846,613 relationships* covering 203,437 biomarkers, 1,161 conditions and 22,633 publications.

== Modelling

=== Data Model

.Biomarker discovery data model
image::life-sciences/research-development/biomarker-discovery-model.svg[Biomarker discovery data model,width=900]

==== Nodes

* `Biomarker` - a single biomarker claim, keyed by `id`. `name` is the human-readable form ("increased VEGF level", "BRCA2 TRUNCATING MUTATION") and `biomarker_controlled_vocab` is the structured phrasing the source curated ("Increased level of protein vascular endothelial growth factor/NCIt:C92514").
* `Gene`, `Protein`, `Metabolite`, `Variant` - the *assessed entity*: what is physically measured. Keyed by a namespaced `id` (`NCBI:672`, `UPKB:P01375`, `LOINC:15035-9`, `dbSNP:rs11263763`). A `loinc` property carries the clinical lab code where one exists.
* `Condition` - the disease the biomarker indicates, identified by a Disease Ontology term (`DOID:1612`). Conditions that also exist in the imported ontology carry a second `:DOID` label  (Disease Ontology) along with the term's `definition`, `synonyms` and `alt_ids`.
* `DOID` - Disease Ontology terms that are not themselves the subject of a biomarker claim, present so that the hierarchy is complete.
* `Specimen` - where the measurement is taken, as an UBERON term (`UBERON:0001977` serum, `UBERON:0001088` urine).
* `Role` - the clinical role of the claim: `diagnostic`, `prognostic`, `monitoring`, `predictive`, `risk`, `safety`, `response`.
* `ExposureAgent` - for exposure biomarkers, the chemical or agent involved.
* `Publication` - a PubMed record, keyed by `pmid`, carrying `title`, `year`, `doi`, `abstract` and (optionally) an `embedding` vector. Also labelled `:Xref`, because a citation is one kind of evidence reference.
* `Xref` - any other cross-reference, keyed by its prefixed `name`. The prefix identifies the vocabulary, and it serves two distinct purposes: source-database evidence for a biomarker (`CIViC:131`, `ClinVar:...`), and terminology codes for a condition (`ICD10CM:C50`, `SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01:254837009`, `UMLS_CUI:C0006142`, `MESH:D001943`). The second kind is what lets the graph join to EHR and claims data.
* `MeshTerm` - a MeSH descriptor used to index a publication, with its `tree_numbers` and corpus-wide `publication_count`.

==== Relationships

* `(:Biomarker)-[:ASSESSES]->(:Gene|:Protein|:Metabolite|:Variant)` - what the biomarker measures. A GWAS biomarker carries two of these: one to the gene and one to the variant.
* `(:Biomarker)-[:INDICATES]->(:Condition)` - the disease the claim is about.
* `(:Biomarker)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(:Role)` - one per clinical role; a biomarker can hold several.
* `(:Biomarker)-[:MEASURED_IN]->(:Specimen)` - the sample type the measurement was reported in.
* `(:Biomarker)-[:EXPOSED_TO]->(:ExposureAgent)` - the agent, for exposure biomarkers.
* `(:Biomarker)-[:REFERENCES]->(:Publication|:Xref)` - the supporting evidence.
* `(:Condition|:DOID)-[:REFERENCES]->(:Xref)` - the terminology codes a condition maps to. 903 of 1,161 conditions carry at least one: 771 a UMLS CUI, 711 SNOMED, 460 ICD-10-CM.
* `(:Publication)-[:HAS_MESH_TERM]->(:MeshTerm)` - MeSH indexing, with `major_topic` and `qualifier_ids` on the relationship.
* `(:Condition|:DOID)-[:IS_A]->(:Condition|:DOID)` and `(:MeshTerm)-[:IS_A]->(:MeshTerm)` - the two ontology hierarchies, which make roll-up queries possible.

==== Two Things the Real Data Will Do to You

Both are worth knowing before you draw conclusions from a count.

*The roles are extremely skewed.* Of 203,437 biomarkers in the full graph, 199,470 hold the `risk` role - overwhelmingly germline variants from clinical-genomics and GWAS curation. Only 2,494 are `diagnostic`, 712 `prognostic`, 154 `monitoring` and 28 `predictive`. Any query that does not exclude `risk` returns a list of variants and buries the clinically actionable markers. The demo data below deliberately caps risk markers so that the rest of the graph is visible at all - see the note under Demo Data.

*The same entity identifier can appear under more than one label.* 105 assessed-entity identifiers exist as two node types at once, because different source datasets declared different entity types for the same accession. `NCBI:11186` (RASSF1) is both a `:Gene` and a `:Protein` - it appears in both node blocks of the demo data below. This is a genuine integration defect in the source data, not a modelling choice, and the graph is the easiest place to find it - `ACE2` surfaces twice in the panel query in question 5 for exactly this reason. Resolving it is a connected-components problem, covered under Graph Data Science below.

=== Demo Data

The script below is the reference demo subgraph shipped with the BiomarkerKB loader, reproduced verbatim. It is seeded on three cancers - breast (`DOID:1612`), pancreatic (`DOID:1793`) and prostate (`DOID:10283`) - and exports the *node-induced* subgraph around them: every relationship whose endpoints were both sampled. That picks up all relationship types automatically and can never emit a dangling edge.

It builds *2,636 nodes and 6,809 relationships*, and loads in four blocks - schema, nodes, relationships, vectors:

[cols="1,1,3", options="header"]
|===
| Label | Count | Notes
| `Biomarker` | 268 | 197 non-risk, plus risk markers capped at 25 per seed
| `Gene` | 110 | assessed entities
| `Protein` | 117 | assessed entities
| `Metabolite` | 16 | assessed entities
| `Variant` | 3 | assessed entities
| `Condition:DOID` | 6 | the three seeds and their sibling terms
| `DOID` | 11 | ontology-only ancestors, closed transitively
| `Specimen` | 12 | UBERON terms
| `Role` | 5 | diagnostic, prognostic, risk, monitoring, predictive
| `Publication:Xref` | 206 | capped at 3 per biomarker, titles and years without abstracts
| `Xref` | 252 | 131 source cross-references (capped at 3 per biomarker) plus 121 condition terminology codes
| `MeshTerm` | 1,630 | 735 indexed terms plus 895 ancestors, closed transitively
|===

Five things about how it was sampled are worth knowing, because each one is forced by the data:

* *Risk markers are capped, everything else is taken whole.* The three seeds reach roughly 17,000 risk biomarkers against about 200 diagnostic, prognostic, monitoring and predictive ones. An uncapped sample would be nothing but germline variants and every clinically interesting query below would come back empty.
* *Both ontologies are closed transitively.* A `Condition` is exported with its Disease Ontology ancestors and a `MeshTerm` with its MeSH ancestors, otherwise the `IS_A` roll-up query silently returns nothing.
* *Condition terminology codes are sampled explicitly.* ICD-10-CM, SNOMED, MeSH and UMLS codes hang off the `Condition`, not off the `Biomarker`, so a biomarker-driven walk misses them. Without them the whitespace, billing and cohort questions below all return nothing.
* *Publication vectors are narrowed, not dropped.* At the full 1,536 dimensions the 206 vectors would be about 2.6 MB of Cypher, several times the rest of the export. `text-embedding-3-small` is a Matryoshka embedding, so a leading 512-dimension slice is still valid once re-normalised: that is a third of the size and holds recall@10 at 0.998 on this corpus. Four decimals is the other half of the saving, and is measured-safe; three decimals is not. Omit `--embeddings` to skip the fourth block entirely - only question 9 needs it.
* *Four bulky properties are omitted, none of which any query below reads.* Publication `abstract`, MeshTerm `tree_numbers`, and `major_topic` and `qualifier_ids` on `HAS_MESH_TERM` together accounted for more than half the export. Dropping them leaves the sample structurally identical - the same 2,636 nodes and 6,809 relationships - so every result on this page is unchanged. The loader's `--drop` flag controls this; omit it to export them.

==== Constraints and Indexes

The header records exactly how the sample was drawn. The constraints that follow are what make the `MERGE` statements cheap: each one backs a lookup that would otherwise be a full scan.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// BiomarkerKB demo subgraph — generated by sample_subgraph.py
// generated:   2026-08-21 13:39:47
// seeds:       DOID:1612, DOID:1793, DOID:10283
// caps:        risk<=25/seed, xrefs<=3/biomarker, publications<=3/biomarker
// nodes:       2,636   relationships: 6,809
// embeddings:  206 vectors, 512 dims, rounded to 4 decimals
// dropped:     HAS_MESH_TERM.major_topic, HAS_MESH_TERM.qualifier_ids, MeshTerm.tree_numbers, Publication.abstract  (7,815 values)
// Idempotent (MERGE-based). Run with:
//   cypher-shell -a <uri> -u neo4j -p <password> -f <this file>

// ---- schema ----
CREATE CONSTRAINT biomarker_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Biomarker) REQUIRE n.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT condition_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Condition) REQUIRE n.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT doid_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:DOID) REQUIRE n.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE INDEX id_Gene IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Gene) ON (n.id);
CREATE CONSTRAINT mesh_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:MeshTerm) REQUIRE n.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE INDEX id_Metabolite IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Metabolite) ON (n.id);
CREATE INDEX id_Protein IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Protein) ON (n.id);
CREATE CONSTRAINT publication_pmid IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Publication) REQUIRE n.pmid IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT role_name IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Role) REQUIRE n.name IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT specimen_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Specimen) REQUIRE n.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE INDEX assessed_biomarker_entity_id_Variant IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Variant) ON (n.assessed_biomarker_entity_id);
CREATE INDEX name_Xref IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:Xref) ON (n.name);
----

==== Nodes

One `UNWIND` batch per label, keyed on the property the constraint covers, with the remaining properties applied through `SET n += row.p`. Note `NCBI:11186` appearing in both the `Gene` and the `Protein` batch - the duplicate identifier described above.

The `MeshTerm` batch is the bulk of it: 1,630 descriptors, most of them ancestors pulled in to complete the hierarchy rather than terms any publication is indexed with directly.

CALL db.create.setNodeVectorProperty(p, 'embedding', row.v);

CREATE VECTOR INDEX publication_embedding IF NOT EXISTS

OPTIONS {indexConfig: {`vector.dimensions`: 512, `vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'}};

CALL db.awaitIndexes(300);
----


== Example Queries

=== 1. Which of our pipeline targets already have a human biomarker, and in what indications?

The first question asked of any target list. A target with existing human biomarker evidence carries less translational risk - and the breadth of that evidence is itself a signal, because a gene marked across a hundred indications is telling you something different from one marked in two.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Existing human biomarker evidence for a target list
UNWIND ['TP53', 'BRAF', 'KRAS', 'ERBB2', 'PIK3CA', 'EGFR'] AS target
MATCH
      (g:Gene {name: target})<-[:ASSESSES]-(b:Biomarker)-[:INDICATES]->(c:Condition)
RETURN
      target AS Target,
      count(DISTINCT c) AS Indications,
      count(DISTINCT b) AS Claims,
      collect(DISTINCT c.name)[0..3] AS Examples
ORDER BY Indications DESC;
----

[cols="1,1,1,3", options="header"]
|===
| Target | Indications | Claims | Examples
| ERBB2 | 2 | 15 | breast cancer, pancreatic cancer
| TP53 | 1 | 8 | breast cancer
| BRAF | 1 | 2 | pancreatic cancer
| KRAS | 1 | 3 | pancreatic cancer
| PIK3CA | 1 | 5 | breast cancer
|===

Note the gap between indications and claims: ERBB2 carries 15 claims across the two indications in this sample, TP53 eight across one. Claim count and indication count are different signals, and the ratio between them is what matters. On the full graph the contrast is stark - EGFR has 2,006 claims across only 59 indications, deep and concentrated, while TP53 has 2,755 spread across 113, the profile of a marker that is everywhere and therefore specific to nothing. Specificity is what separates the two, and it is a graph aggregation: the count of other conditions reachable from the same assessed entity.

=== 2. If we own a marker in one indication, where else could it read out?

Label extension. The marker is already validated and the assay already exists, so the question is purely which other indication could reuse it. Existing evidence in a neighbouring disease is the cheapest possible signal, and the ontology says how near the neighbour is.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Indications where a marker we already own has evidence elsewhere
WITH 'DOID:1612' as breast_cancer
MATCH
      (g:Gene {name: 'BRCA1'})<-[:ASSESSES]-(:Biomarker)-[:INDICATES]->(owned:Condition {id: breast_cancer})
WITH g, owned
MATCH (g)<-[:ASSESSES]-(b2:Biomarker)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(r:Role)
WHERE r.name <> 'risk'
MATCH (b2)-[:INDICATES]->(other:Condition)
WHERE other <> owned
OPTIONAL MATCH
      path = (other)-[:IS_A*1..4]->(shared)<-[:IS_A*1..4]-(owned)
WITH
      other,
      count(DISTINCT b2) AS claims,
      collect(DISTINCT r.name) AS roles,
      min(length(path)) AS hops
RETURN
      other.name AS `Candidate Indication`,
      claims AS Claims,
      roles AS Roles,
      hops AS `Ontology Hops`
ORDER BY Claims DESC, `Candidate Indication`
LIMIT 8;
----

[cols="2,1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Candidate Indication | Claims | Roles | Ontology Hops
| prostate cancer | 1 | prognostic | 4
|===

NOTE: The same expansion works through either hierarchy. Rolling up the MeSH term `D009369` (Neoplasms) reaches 82 descendant terms and 231 biomarkers in this sample, and *525 terms and 58,104 biomarkers* on the full graph - the whole oncology evidence base from one node:

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Everything under one MeSH branch
WITH 'D009369' as neoplasms
MATCH
      (root:MeshTerm {id: neoplasms})<-[:IS_A*0..]-(m:MeshTerm)
WITH collect(DISTINCT m) AS terms
UNWIND terms AS m
MATCH
      (m)<-[:HAS_MESH_TERM]-(:Publication)<-[:REFERENCES]-(b:Biomarker)
RETURN
      size(terms) AS `MeSH Terms`,
      count(DISTINCT b) AS Biomarkers;
----

=== 3. Where is the diagnostic whitespace?

High literature interest with thin biomarker coverage is where an unmet need lives. The trap is that a naive count per `Condition` measures term-splitting, not whitespace: "colorectal carcinoma" and "colorectal cancer" are separate Disease Ontology terms and the markers land on one of them. Normalising through the shared MeSH descriptor fixes it, and the `DOID Terms` column shows how many source terms were merged.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Literature interest versus actionable marker coverage, normalised on MeSH
MATCH (c:Condition)-[:REFERENCES]->(x:Xref)
WHERE x.name STARTS WITH 'MESH:'
MATCH (m:MeshTerm {id: split(x.name, ':')[1]})
OPTIONAL MATCH
      (c)<-[:INDICATES]-(b:Biomarker)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(r:Role)
      WHERE r.name <> 'risk'
WITH  m,
      collect(DISTINCT c.name) AS doidTerms,
      count(DISTINCT b) AS markers
WHERE m.publication_count >= 300
RETURN
      m.name AS Disease,
      m.publication_count AS Literature,
      markers AS `Actionable Markers`,
      size(doidTerms) AS `DOID Terms`,
      round(1.0 * m.publication_count / (markers + 1), 1) AS `Papers per Marker`
ORDER BY `Papers per Marker` DESC
LIMIT 10;
----

[cols="2,1,1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Disease | Literature | Actionable Markers | DOID Terms | Papers per Marker
| Neoplasms | 881 | 0 | 1 | 881.0
| Breast Neoplasms | 2724 | 100 | 1 | 27.0
| Pancreatic Neoplasms | 421 | 36 | 1 | 11.4
| Prostatic Neoplasms | 373 | 61 | 1 | 6.0
|===

Prostate is the saturated end of this sample at 6 papers per marker and breast at 27. `Neoplasms` heads the list with 881 papers and no actionable markers of its own, because it is the roll-up parent rather than an indication anyone curates against - the top row is an artefact of the hierarchy, not a finding. On the full graph the same query surfaces real whitespace: brain tumours at 111 papers per marker, and histology labels such as "Adenocarcinoma" that are curation artefacts rather than indications.

=== 4. Can this biomarker be measured non-invasively?

No liquid-biopsy path means a biopsy, and a biopsy changes the entire commercial case for a test. The `MEASURED_IN` edge answers it directly - with one important caveat.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Does each candidate have a liquid-biopsy path?
UNWIND ['Mucin-1', 'TP53', 'Carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecule 5',
        'Prostate Specific Antigen', 'Interleukin-6'] AS target
MATCH
      (e {name: target})<-[:ASSESSES]-(b:Biomarker)
OPTIONAL MATCH
      (b)-[:MEASURED_IN]->(s:Specimen)
WITH
      target,
      count(DISTINCT b) AS claims,
      collect(DISTINCT s.name) AS specimens
RETURN
      target AS Entity,
      claims AS Claims,
      [x IN specimens WHERE x IN ['blood', 'serum', 'plasma', 'urine', 'cerebrospinal fluid']] AS `Liquid Biopsy`,
      [x IN specimens WHERE NOT x IN ['blood', 'serum', 'plasma', 'urine', 'cerebrospinal fluid']] AS Other
ORDER BY size(`Liquid Biopsy`) DESC, Entity;
----

[cols="2,1,2,2", options="header"]
|===
| Entity | Claims | Liquid Biopsy | Other
| Prostate Specific Antigen | 1 | serum, plasma | 
| Carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecule 5 | 1 | blood | 
| Interleukin-6 | 3 | blood | 
| Mucin-1 | 1 | blood | 
| TP53 | 8 |  | 
|===

Across the whole graph the fluid specimens are urine 785 biomarkers, blood 745, serum 530, plasma 470 and cerebrospinal fluid 77.

IMPORTANT: There are only 3,522 `MEASURED_IN` edges against 203,437 biomarkers. *Absence of a specimen is missing curation, not evidence of a tissue-only marker.* Treat this query as a positive filter - it confirms a liquid-biopsy path exists, it never rules one out.

=== 5. What is the minimum marker panel covering the most patients in indication X?

A set-cover problem over the entity-to-condition bipartite graph. Before it can be solved, the indication has to be reconciled: on the full graph, pancreatic cancer's actionable markers are split across six Disease Ontology terms, and conditions are keyed under three different vocabularies (961 `DOID`, 195 `MONDO`, 5 `OMIM`). The `IS_A` rollup unifies them.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Panel candidates across every subtype term of one indication
WITH 'DOID:1793' as pancreatic_cancer
MATCH (root:Condition {id: pancreatic_cancer})<-[:IS_A*0..3]-(c:Condition)
MATCH (c)<-[:INDICATES]-(b:Biomarker)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(r:Role)
WHERE r.name <> 'risk'
MATCH (b)-[:ASSESSES]->(e)
OPTIONAL MATCH
      (b)-[:MEASURED_IN]->(s:Specimen)
WITH
      e,
      count(DISTINCT b) AS claims,
      collect(DISTINCT c.name) AS terms,
      collect(DISTINCT s.name) AS specimens
RETURN
      e.name AS Entity,
      claims AS Claims,
      size(terms) AS `Subtype Terms Covered`,
      specimens AS Specimens
ORDER BY Claims DESC, Entity
LIMIT 6;
----

[cols="2,1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Entity | Claims | Subtype Terms Covered | Specimens
| KRAS | 2 | 1 | 
| SAA1 | 2 | 1 | blood
| 26S proteasome non-ATPase regulatory subunit 11 | 1 | 1 | blood
| ACE2 | 1 | 1 | pancreas
| ACE2 | 1 | 1 | pancreas
| APOA1 | 1 | 1 | 
|===

Every entity covers a single subtype term here, because the sampled pancreatic seed has no descendant terms - set cover only becomes an interesting problem once the full ontology is present, where KRAS alone covers four of the six subtype terms and nothing else covers more than two. What this sample does show is the duplicate-identifier defect: `ACE2` appears twice, once as a `:Gene` and once as a `:Protein`, exactly as described in the modelling section.

The reconciliation is worth seeing on its own, on the full graph. `DOID:3498` "pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma" carries three actionable markers but is *not* a descendant of `DOID:1793` in this ontology, so the rollup above misses it. A string search finds it; the hierarchy does not. It falls outside the sampled subgraph, so it is not reproducible from the demo data.

=== 6. Is this marker's evidence one paper or fifty, and how recent?

Evidence depth and evidence currency are different risks. A marker with one supporting paper from 2008 is a different proposition from one with ten papers through 2019, even if both are "published".

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Depth and currency of the evidence behind each candidate
WITH 'DOID:1612' as breast_cancer
MATCH (c:Condition {id: breast_cancer})<-[:INDICATES]-(b:Biomarker)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(r:Role)
WHERE r.name <> 'risk'
MATCH (b)-[:ASSESSES]->(e)
OPTIONAL MATCH
      (b)-[:REFERENCES]->(p:Publication)
WITH
      e,
      count(DISTINCT p) AS papers,
      min(p.year) AS first,
      max(p.year) AS latest
WHERE papers > 0
RETURN
      e.name AS Entity,
      papers AS Papers,
      first AS First,
      latest AS Latest,
      2026 - latest AS `Years Stale`
ORDER BY Papers DESC, Entity
LIMIT 8;
----

[cols="2,1,1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Entity | Papers | First | Latest | Years Stale
| PIK3CA | 6 | 2007 | 2011 | 15
| TP53 | 5 | 1998 | 2012 | 14
| PGR | 3 | 2006 | 2013 | 13
| BRCA1 | 2 | 2005 | 2013 | 13
| BRCA2 | 2 | 2005 | 2008 | 18
| CD274 | 2 | 2017 | 2017 | 9
| Mucin-1 | 2 | 2010 | 2014 | 12
| Vascular endothelial growth factor | 2 | 2009 | 2013 | 13
|===

Read the `Years Stale` column against the curation, not the science. The corpus itself has a currency cliff: in this sample the count falls from 16 publications dated 2016 to a single one in 2024, and the full graph shows the same shape at scale - 1,206 publications carry a 2020 date, 940 in 2021, 642 in 2022, 266 in 2023, 79 in 2024 and 72 in 2025. A stale marker may simply be one the curators have not revisited:

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Currency of the supporting corpus
MATCH (:Biomarker)-[:REFERENCES]->(p:Publication)
WHERE p.year >= 2016
RETURN
      p.year AS Year,
      count(DISTINCT p) AS Publications
ORDER BY Year;
----

=== 7. Is it billable and reportable?

A marker that cannot be coded cannot be reimbursed. That means a LOINC code on the analyte and an ICD-10-CM or SNOMED code on the indication.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Codeable markers and the codes for their indication
MATCH (c:Condition {id: 'DOID:1612'})<-[:INDICATES]-(b:Biomarker)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(r:Role)
WHERE r.name <> 'risk'
MATCH (b)-[:ASSESSES]->(e)
WHERE e.loinc IS NOT NULL AND e.loinc <> ''
OPTIONAL MATCH
      (c)-[:REFERENCES]->(x:Xref)
      WHERE split(x.name, ':')[0] IN ['ICD10CM', 'SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01']
WITH e, collect(DISTINCT x.name) AS codes
RETURN
      e.name AS Entity,
      e.loinc AS LOINC,
      codes[0..2] AS `Condition Codes`
ORDER BY Entity
LIMIT 6;
----

[cols="2,1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Entity | LOINC | Condition Codes
| Alanine aminotransferase 1 | 76625-3 | ICD10CM:C50, SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01:254837009
| CCND1 | 21744-8 | ICD10CM:C50, SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01:254837009
| Calcium Oxalate (CaOx) | 15085-4 | ICD10CM:C50, SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01:254837009
| Calcium Oxalate (CaOx) | 14862-7 | ICD10CM:C50, SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01:254837009
| Calcium Oxalate (CaOx) | 14861-9 | ICD10CM:C50, SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01:254837009
| Calcium Oxalate (CaOx) | 15086-2 | ICD10CM:C50, SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01:254837009
|===

LOINC coverage across the graph is heavily lopsided, and it changes where a diagnostics programme should look:

[cols="1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Entity Type | Entities | With LOINC
| Gene | 10499 | 57
| Protein | 457 | 104
| Metabolite | 836 | 731
|===

The metabolites are 87% coded because they came from LOINC-derived clinical chemistry in the first place. Genes are at 0.5%. Today's billable layer is overwhelmingly clinical chemistry, not genomics - which is a statement about coding infrastructure, not about clinical value.

=== 8. Can we join this to our own RWD/EHR and trial data?

The cross-reference layer is the bridge. A condition's SNOMED and ICD-10-CM codes are what an EHR query needs, and the LOINC codes are what a lab feed carries - so a cohort can be sized against real-world data before a protocol is written.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Cohort definition for one indication and its subtypes
WITH 'DOID:1612' as breast_cancer
MATCH (root:Condition {id: breast_cancer})<-[:IS_A*0..2]-(c:Condition)
MATCH (c)-[:REFERENCES]->(x:Xref)
WITH
      split(x.name, ':')[0] AS vocabulary,
      collect(DISTINCT x.name) AS codes
RETURN
      vocabulary AS Vocabulary,
      size(codes) AS Codes,
      codes[0..2] AS Examples
ORDER BY Vocabulary;
----

[cols="1,1,3", options="header"]
|===
| Vocabulary | Codes | Examples
| ICD10CM | 1 | ICD10CM:C50
| MESH | 1 | MESH:D001943
| MIM | 1 | MIM:114480
| NCI | 1 | NCI:C9335
| SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01 | 1 | SNOMEDCT_US_2025_09_01:254837009
| UMLS_CUI | 1 | UMLS_CUI:C0006142
|===

Coverage of the bridge is the thing to check before relying on it. Of 1,161 conditions, 903 carry at least one code: 771 have a UMLS CUI, 711 have SNOMED, and only 460 have ICD-10-CM. An ICD-10-only join silently drops 60% of the indications in the graph.

=== 9. "Find me emerging early-detection markers for pancreatic cancer"

Asked in plain English. The question is embedded with the same model used on the corpus, the vector index finds the 50 semantically closest publications, and the graph turns those papers into ranked entities. 

NOTE: This is the one question that needs the fourth load block above, which stores the vectors and creates the index.

In the reference build 22,625 publications were embedded with `text-embedding-3-small` at 1,536 dimensions over title, abstract and MeSH descriptor names; the demo export narrows that to the leading 512 dimensions. `$queryVector` below is the question run through the same model - and it must be narrowed and re-normalised the same way, or the widths will not match the index.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Plain-English question -> nearest publications -> ranked entities
// $queryVector is "Find me emerging early-detection markers for pancreatic cancer",
// embedded with the same model and narrowed to the same 512 dimensions as the corpus
WITH 50 as numberOfNeighbors
CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes('publication_embedding', numberOfNeighbors, $queryVector)
YIELD node AS p, score
MATCH (p)<-[:REFERENCES]-(b:Biomarker)-[:ASSESSES]->(e)
MATCH (b)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(r:Role)
WITH
      coalesce(e.name, e.assessed_biomarker_entity_id) AS entity, p, r, score
RETURN
      entity AS Entity,
      count(DISTINCT p) AS Papers,
      collect(DISTINCT r.name) AS Roles,
      round(max(score), 3) AS `Best Match`
ORDER BY Papers DESC, Entity
LIMIT 8;
----

[cols="1,1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Entity | Papers | Roles | Best Match
| ERBB2 | 2 | risk | 0.753
| KRAS | 2 | prognostic | 0.759
| RRM1 | 2 | risk | 0.78
| SAA1 | 2 | monitoring | 0.789
| ST6GALNAC6 | 2 | diagnostic | 0.769
| Serum amyloid A-1 protein | 2 | monitoring | 0.789
| TYMS | 2 | prognostic, risk | 0.77
| 26S proteasome non-ATPase regulatory subunit 11 | 1 | prognostic | 0.816
|===

The semantic search worked, and the list it returns is a mixture. ERBB2 and RRM1 come back on `risk` claims alone and TYMS on a risk claim alongside a prognostic one - susceptibility and chemo-sensitivity genes, not early-detection markers. The literature discusses them alongside early detection, so the embedding places them together. On the full graph, where 98% of biomarkers carry the `risk` role, the effect is far stronger and the unfiltered list is almost entirely predisposition genes.

The graph is what catches it. Adding the `risk` exclusion that every other query on this page applies - for the reason set out under the role skew above - changes the answer completely:

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// The same question, with the role filter applied
// $queryVector is "Find me emerging early-detection markers for pancreatic cancer",
// embedded with the same model and narrowed to the same 512 dimensions as the corpus
WITH 50 as numberOfNeighbors
CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes('publication_embedding', numberOfNeighbors, $queryVector)
YIELD node AS p, score
MATCH (p)<-[:REFERENCES]-(b:Biomarker)-[:ASSESSES]->(e)
MATCH (b)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(r:Role)
WHERE r.name <> 'risk'
WITH
      coalesce(e.name, e.assessed_biomarker_entity_id) AS entity, p, r, score
RETURN
      entity AS Entity,
      count(DISTINCT p) AS Papers,
      collect(DISTINCT r.name) AS Roles,
      round(max(score), 3) AS `Best Match`
ORDER BY Papers DESC, Entity
LIMIT 6;
----

[cols="2,1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Entity | Papers | Roles | Best Match
| KRAS | 2 | prognostic | 0.759
| SAA1 | 2 | monitoring | 0.789
| ST6GALNAC6 | 2 | diagnostic | 0.769
| Serum amyloid A-1 protein | 2 | monitoring | 0.789
| 26S proteasome non-ATPase regulatory subunit 11 | 1 | prognostic | 0.816
| 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine | 1 | diagnostic | 0.754
|===

IMPORTANT: This is the argument for GraphRAG in one table. Vector search cannot tell a susceptibility gene from an early-detection marker, because nothing in the text marks the difference; the curated structure supplies the constraint - `role <> 'risk'` - that a language model has no way to infer. Every row is anchored to specific PMIDs, so the answer can be cited rather than asserted. At demo scale the filter clears three entities off the top of the list; on the full graph it changes the answer outright.

NOTE: `Papers` counts scale with the `k` passed to `queryNodes` - it is a ranking signal, not an absolute. The vector index also only covers publications that were embedded, so candidates supported solely by database cross-references are invisible here. This complements the curated traversals rather than replacing them.

== Graph Data Science

The queries above answer questions about one disease at a time. Graph algorithms answer questions about the shape of the whole evidence network.

The projections below assume a Neo4j deployment with the Graph Data Science library. On AuraDB with Graph Analytics Serverless the algorithm calls are the same, but the projection is created from a GDS Session rather than from the database.

NOTE: A Cypher projection is held in memory under the name you give it, separately from the database, and it stays there until it is dropped or the DBMS restarts. Running any of the projection statements below a second time therefore fails with `Graph condition-entity already exists` instead of rebuilding it. Drop it first with `CALL gds.graph.drop('condition-entity', false)` - the `false` means "do not fail if it is missing", so the call is safe on a clean database - or guard the projection with `CALL gds.graph.exists(...) YIELD exists WITH exists WHERE NOT exists`. The same applies in reverse: because a projection is a snapshot, one left in memory will keep serving stale results after the underlying data has changed.

=== Which diseases share biology?

Project a bipartite graph of conditions and the entities they are marked by, then run *Node Similarity*. Diseases that come out similar share assessed entities, which is exactly the signal a repurposing or platform-assay strategy is looking for.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// A projection lives in memory under its name, so re-running this against a
// projection left over from an earlier run fails with "Graph condition-entity
// already exists". Drop it first; `false` means do not fail if it is absent.
CALL gds.graph.drop('condition-entity', false) YIELD graphName RETURN graphName;

// Project conditions and the entities marking them
MATCH (c:Condition)<-[:INDICATES]-(b:Biomarker)-[:ASSESSES]->(e)
WHERE NOT (b)-[:HAS_ROLE]->(:Role {name: 'risk'})
RETURN gds.graph.project(
  'condition-entity',
  c,
  e,
  {sourceNodeLabels: ['Condition'], targetNodeLabels: labels(e), relationshipType: 'MARKED_BY'},
  {undirectedRelationshipTypes: ['MARKED_BY']}
);

// Diseases that share the most assessed entities
CALL gds.nodeSimilarity.stream('condition-entity', {topK: 5})
YIELD node1, node2, similarity
WITH gds.util.asNode(node1) AS a, gds.util.asNode(node2) AS b, similarity
WHERE a:Condition AND b:Condition
RETURN
      a.name AS Condition,
      b.name AS `Similar Condition`,
      round(similarity, 3) AS Similarity
ORDER BY Similarity DESC
LIMIT 20;
----

[cols="2,2,1", options="header"]
|===
| Condition | Similar Condition | Similarity
| pancreatic cancer | prostate cancer | 0.025
| prostate cancer | pancreatic cancer | 0.025
| breast cancer | pancreatic cancer | 0.021
| pancreatic cancer | breast cancer | 0.021
| breast cancer | prostate cancer | 0.017
| prostate cancer | breast cancer | 0.017
|===

=== Which entities are hubs, and which are peripheral?

*Degree centrality* over the same projection separates the general-purpose analytes - inflammation markers, TP53 - from the ones tied to a single indication. A high-degree entity is a poor standalone diagnostic and a good panel component; a low-degree entity with deep evidence is the specific candidate a programme wants.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Entities ranked by how many conditions they mark
CALL gds.degree.stream('condition-entity')
YIELD nodeId, score
WITH gds.util.asNode(nodeId) AS n, score
WHERE NOT n:Condition
RETURN
      n.name AS Entity,
      labels(n)[0] AS Type,
      toInteger(score) AS Conditions
ORDER BY Conditions DESC
LIMIT 20;
----

[cols="2,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Entity | Type | Conditions
| TP53 | Gene | 6
| Interleukin-6 | Protein | 3
| Zinc-alpha-2-glycoprotein | Protein | 3
| PIK3CA | Gene | 3
| CHEK2 | Gene | 3
| RASSF1 | Protein | 2
| MKI67 | Gene | 2
| ST6GALNAC6 | Protein | 2
| Serum amyloid A-1 protein | Protein | 2
| KRAS | Gene | 2
| ABCB1 | Gene | 2
| ST6GALNAC6 | Gene | 2
| BRCA1 | Gene | 2
| RASSF1 | Gene | 2
| BRCA2 | Gene | 2
| NCOA3 | Gene | 2
| Interleukin-8 | Protein | 2
| SAA1 | Gene | 2
| Calcium Oxalate (CaOx) | Metabolite | 1
| Calcium Oxalate (CaOx) | Metabolite | 1

=== Where are the research communities?

*Louvain* over the publication and MeSH co-indexing network groups the literature into research themes. Mapping candidates onto those communities shows whether a shortlist is genuinely diverse or whether every candidate comes from the same body of work - a common and expensive form of confirmation bias in biomarker programmes.

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// A projection lives in memory under its name, so re-running this against a
// projection left over from an earlier run fails with "Graph literature
// already exists". Drop it first; `false` means do not fail if it is absent.
CALL gds.graph.drop('literature', false) YIELD graphName RETURN graphName;

// Project the literature co-indexing network
MATCH
      (p:Publication)-[:HAS_MESH_TERM]->(m:MeshTerm)
RETURN gds.graph.project(
  'literature',
  p,
  m,
  {sourceNodeLabels: ['Publication'], targetNodeLabels: ['MeshTerm'], relationshipType: 'INDEXED_AS'},
  {undirectedRelationshipTypes: ['INDEXED_AS']}
);

// Research communities, and how many biomarkers each one supports
CALL gds.louvain.stream('literature')
YIELD nodeId, communityId
WITH communityId, gds.util.asNode(nodeId) AS n
WHERE n:Publication
MATCH (n)<-[:REFERENCES]-(b:Biomarker)
RETURN
      communityId AS Community,
      count(DISTINCT n) AS Publications,
      count(DISTINCT b) AS Biomarkers
ORDER BY Biomarkers DESC
LIMIT 10;
----

[cols="1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
| Community | Publications | Biomarkers
| 926 | 52 | 77
| 393 | 22 | 33
| 413 | 22 | 27
| 536 | 14 | 24
| 840 | 23 | 16
| 810 | 9 | 14
| 642 | 4 | 14
| 662 | 9 | 12
| 875 | 10 | 12
| 543 | 11 | 12
|===

=== Resolving duplicated entities

The 105 duplicated identifiers described in the modelling section are a connected-components problem once the candidate equivalences are materialised. Project entities linked by shared identifier or normalised name, run *Weakly Connected Components*, and every component with more than one member is a resolution candidate for a curator to confirm - the same approach described in xref:agnostic/entity-resolution.adoc[Entity Resolution].

[source, cypher, role=noheader]
----
// Candidate equivalences: same id under a different label, or the same normalised name
MATCH (a), (b)
WHERE (a:Gene OR a:Protein OR a:Metabolite)
  AND (b:Gene OR b:Protein OR b:Metabolite)
  AND elementId(a) < elementId(b)
  AND (a.id = b.id OR toLower(trim(a.name)) = toLower(trim(b.name)))
MERGE (a)-[:SAME_AS_CANDIDATE]-(b);

// A projection lives in memory under its name, so re-running this against a
// projection left over from an earlier run fails with "Graph entity-resolution
// already exists". Drop it first; `false` means do not fail if it is absent.
CALL gds.graph.drop('entity-resolution', false) YIELD graphName RETURN graphName;

// Project those candidate edges, undirected - WCC needs both directions
MATCH (a)-[:SAME_AS_CANDIDATE]-(b)
RETURN gds.graph.project(
  'entity-resolution',
  a,
  b,
  {},
  {undirectedRelationshipTypes: ['*']}
);

CALL gds.wcc.stream('entity-resolution')
YIELD nodeId, componentId
WITH componentId, collect(gds.util.asNode(nodeId).name) AS members
WHERE size(members) > 1
RETURN componentId AS Component, members AS Members
ORDER BY size(members) DESC
LIMIT 20;
----

| 0 | Calcium Oxalate (CaOx), Calcium Oxalate (CaOx), Calcium Oxalate (CaOx), Calcium Oxalate (CaOx)

== Working With the Full Dataset

The demo excerpt is enough to explore the model. The full graph is where the prioritisation gets interesting, because specificity and evidence depth only mean something when every indication is present.

* *Source data* - https://data.biomarkerkb.org/[data.biomarkerkb.org] publishes each release as TSV. Release v-3.2.2 is 23 TSV files plus two archives, roughly 804 MB. The integrated `masterlist.tsv` carries about 818,000 rows; per-source files (`biomarkers_civic.tsv`, `biomarkers_gwas.tsv`, `biomarkers_clinvar.tsv`, `biomarkers_oncomx.tsv`, `biomarkers_mw_loinc.tsv` and others) can be loaded individually.
* *Project and code* - https://github.com/clinical-biomarkers[github.com/clinical-biomarkers], part of the NIH https://commonfund.nih.gov/dataecosystem[Common Fund Data Ecosystem].
* *Ontologies* - conditions resolve against the https://disease-ontology.org/[Disease Ontology] (`doid.obo`), specimens against https://obophenotype.github.io/uberon/[UBERON], and publications against the https://www.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/[NLM MeSH] release.
* *Literature* - publication records and MeSH indexing come from https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK25501/[NCBI E-utilities].

Two loading notes matter in practice. The `evidence` column of `masterlist.tsv` is long free text and accounts for most of the file size; dropping it and keeping the supporting PubMed citation as a `:Publication` node preserves everything the queries above need. And `LOAD CSV` with `file:///` is unavailable on Aura, so a driver-based loader or the Neo4j Data Importer is the route for a managed instance.

== Where This Leads

The same graph supports the next steps in the programme rather than being rebuilt for each one:

* xref:life-sciences/research-development/multi-omics.adoc[Multi-omics Data Integration] - connect internal experimental measurements to these public candidates so an in-house signal can be checked against prior evidence before anyone commits to it.
* xref:life-sciences/competitive-intelligence/pipeline-intelligence.adoc[Pipeline Intelligence] - see which competitors are running trials against the entities on your shortlist.
* xref:life-sciences/medical-care/patient-journey.adoc[Patient Journey] - link validated markers to the point in a real care pathway where the test would actually be ordered.
